Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) Background: This proposal is requesting the addition of tracks to an existing degree program, the MS in Dietetics. This is being requested because the program is seeking accreditation by its external credentialing agency. We are requesting that the MS degree now has two tracks – one for students completing the accredited program and one for students who are not completing the accredited program. Currently, the degree does not have any tracks. The MS in Dietetics Program has been in existence since 2015. It was created in partnership with Sodexo Dietetic Internship in anticipation of the 2024 entry level 11/28/2021 12/14/2021

2 credentialing requirement which states that all students need a master’s degree with experiential learning to become Registered Dietitian Nutritionists (RDNs).
Until 2024, a BS degree and an internship that provides experiential learning are required to become a RDN.
This change prompted free-standing internships to partner with universities to meet this new degree requirement.
The University of Rhode Island has successfully worked with Sodexo to provide a master’s degree to its interns for the past 6 years.
We are now formalizing the existing partnership with Sodexo by becoming an accredited Future Graduate Program to meet the Future Education Model (FEM) Standards as outlined by the Accreditation Council for Education in Nutrition and Dietetics (ACEND).
The FEM requires enhanced integration between the didactic and experiential components as part of the accreditation.
Curriculum changes to meet the new standards were approved in the spring of 2021.
The FEM Program will begin in the fall of 2022.
Students who complete these requirements need to be in a separate track to best manage our accreditation.
In 2018, URI expanded the master’s degree offering to RDNs employed by Sodexo.

This program was requested by Sodexo to help their current RDNs to remain competitive with new graduates entering the workforce with master’s degrees.
RDNs complete the MS degree in a separate cohort, and complete individualized learning experiences instead of the standard experiential learning rotations.
We are requesting a second non-accredited track in the MS in Dietetics degree to allow us to continue to offer the program to these students and to students who are unable to complete the accredited track.
The MS in Dietetics has graduated 217 students as of December 2021.
Rationale: Tracks need to be added to the MS in Dietetics degree to accommodate students affiliated with Sodexo who will not complete the integrated FEM Program.
Track 1 –Integrated Experiential Track 1.
Students completing the integrated program with alignment between experiential learning and didactic material.
This track will be accredited by an external agency.
Track 2 –Individualized Experiential Track 1.
Students who are RDNs employed by Sodexo who are seeking a master’s degree who have already completed the experiential learning component. 2.
Students with experiential learning timing issues.

As the new accreditation requirements are phased in nationwide, it is possible that a small number of students with off-sequence experiential learning may be able to complete this track and sit for the Registered Dietitian exam more quickly.
This is likely a very small number of students. 3.
Students who are unable to complete the experiential component of the FEM track and need a path to degree completion.
This is also likely to be a very small number of students.

3 courses. Students in FEM track complete 6 credits of experiential learning that is integrated in the program (NFS 571-576). This is not only reflected in the wide variety of double majors that we see in FLM students, but this is also seen in the ways in which they choose to work, or concentrate, within the broad categories of film production: narrative film, documentary production, commercial/corporate work, and art or experimental cinemas.
We emphasize that each of our majors is on a unique path through our major and URI, and their career choices and goals--because the Film/TV industries offer so many different types of work---will be individualized.

Recognizing the nature of this means that Film/Media advisors are focused on enhancing the personal success of each student and appreciating the unique goals that we must help them reach.
Strategy #5: Reframe and redefine liberal education at URI in the context of the 21st century~~ The 21st century has “reframed and redefined” liberal education, and this statement of this strategy is reflective of the ways in which the University is committed as an active participant in these changes.
The Harrington School tagline of “Think.
Create.
Communicate” could not more aptly describe the process of filmmaking, the important

9 nature of collaboration on these projects, and the emphasis on both technical and critical analytical skills that are embodied in the FLM major. “Liberal Education” now often means to our students and their families a grounding in critical reading, critical writing, and critical thinking skills, that must be applied to critical and skillful communication that opens avenues to successful and rewarding careers.
These three tenets of the liberal education project are now, more than ever, being considered in light of hands-on technical and professional skills that our alumni can bring to the jobs they will encounter.
Film/Media is a major with the unique position of offering not only strong communication and analytical skills, but these strengths are added to a wide array of technical job-ready knowledge, aptitude, and experiences that mean that our majors graduate from the University with extremely concrete skills in hand.

Film, itself, for over 125 years, has always been at the forefront of cultural, sociological, and technological breakthroughs, and the major, as a department, should be a visible leader at URI in introducing, experimenting with, and solidifying new ways to teach and learn.

Strategy #4: Involve undergraduate and graduate students in rich and varied research, creative projects and other opportunities~~ Film/Media continues to offer new and innovative courses and topics.

This fully remote, online course allowed students to research, prepare and record broadcasting segments on their reflections on the many vital current issues going on during that difficult year.
Every week those segments were edited together to present a television show that was aired online.

Professor Mary Healey Jamiel developed FLM 444: Filmmakers Professional Portfolio.

Film/Media continues to offer a plethora of special events and opportunities for our students including end-of-the semester student film screenings-- attended by friends and families-- and a wide variety of guest speakers: industry professionals, alumni, and filmmakers with Q&A sessions for our majors.

In the classroom, our topics courses open up ever-changing concentrations on varying aspects of the study of the moving image.

The recognition of Film/Media as a department will introduce resources and recognition for the major to expand these innovative offerings that so richly supplement the academic careers of students in FLM, the Harrington School and URI, and will attract both internal and external partners to develop new potential curriculum initiatives.

Goal #3: Grow a Global Presence: Strategy #3: Create opportunities for the internationalization of the curriculum and co- curriculum to ensure that all students are exposed to global perspectives and build global competence~~ Film/Media holds an essentially central focus in delivering global and international content to our students, and we emphasize the importance of global content in our curriculum in many ways.
One of the foundational aspects of our teaching is that all critical studies courses, including FLM 101, should contain at least 50% international or global films on our syllabi.
Teaching film and TV means that we are focused on global media and on instilling in our students a true understanding of different global perspectives, cultural attitudes, and the ways in which lives, people, and places occupy their spaces in the world and how that relates to our students here in Rhode Island.
Film is a global industry, and the viewing and production of film is usually not defined by geopolitical borders or demarcations.

The Film/Media major is one that must--and does-- always forefront the world in which the film artifact moves and exists, the populations that consume and view it, and the essential importance to our students of understanding the global impact and interconnectivity of what they watch and create.

Film/Media is dedicated to supporting our faculty in their creative work and research and in assuring that this work is seen and applauded internationally.
Our faculty’s wide and ongoing experiences in engaging with geopolitical spaces around the globe, and the wide scope of Film/Media’s international visibility, warrants Departmental recognition for our faculty’s continued contribution to URI’s and the Harrington School’s global footprint.
Goal #4: Embrace Diversity and Social Justice Strategy #2: Increase the recruitment, retention, and graduation of students from underrepresented groups, and provide support for their inclusion and success in the academic environment~~ The Film/Media major is dedicated to Diversity and Social Justice.

This is, of course, reflected in our curriculum as we focus on films and filmmakers that we study from every geography and nation, from all ethnicities, gender identities, and sexual orientations.
As a discipline that is enmeshed in inter-and multi-disciplinary studies, the foundation of FLM relies on --and focuses upon--exposure to different voices and different ways of seeing.
Film/Media is defined by the concept that film and filmmaking is universal, humanistic, and that the making and appreciation of art--and its inclusion in our lives-- is, perhaps, one of the foremost common denominators of the shared human experience.
Recruitment: Film/Media--with the support of the Harrington School-- has pursued for several years the possibility of introducing a program of concurrent enrollment between URI and the JM Walsh School for the Visual and Performing Arts in Pawtucket, RI, so that students at JM Walsh will receive college credit while finishing high school.
This successful

13 proposal allows for the offering of three courses required for the FLM major: FLM 101, 110 and 220 to be taught at JM Walsh to students in their Junior and Senior High School years.
This is an extremely positive step in opening up avenues for diverse students to enter the University with some coursework completed and a foothold into the FLM major.
Beginning in Spring, 2022, our first FLM courses will be held at the JM Walsh school, and we are very much looking forward to working closely with the school to support this curriculum with on-campus events and screenings, and collaborative interactions with our majors.
JM Walsh also offers majors in Art, Music and Theater, and we are hoping that this program will introduce students to the wider Harrington School disciplines and other URI majors as well.
In addition, to aid in recruitment and retention, since 2018, Film/Media has offered FLM 100 and FLM 110 in tandem as part of the summer Talent Development Program (we did not offer this in Summer 2020 because of the difficulties of teaching introductory production remotely during COVID).

Successful recruitment of diverse students will remain problematic without the organizational change for FLM to department status.
Although it is difficult to quantify, it can be assumed that prospective students and families may well be uncertain about committing to a major that is allocated only as a program, and that concern no doubt stems from questions of resource allocations and available institutional support for the major and its students.
In addition, it is no doubt more difficult for our Admissions Office to advocate on behalf of a discipline that has somehow not seen and named as a department.
It is extremely important for FLM to become a department in order to better attract our major to potential students of all backgrounds.
Department status conferred on Film/Media will also strengthen our ability to engage with the community, as we have with JM Walsh and encourage them to participate in often difficult negotiations to institute new and innovative programs.
Inclusion/Retention: Film/Media is committed to diversity, inclusivity and anti-racist principles.

Our topics courses focus on an extensive variety of film from differing geopolitical areas, among filmmakers around the globe, and which address difficult and relevant topics concerning race, gender, economic and social disparities, and the history and ongoing reality of oppression, power, and imperial violence.
Filmmaking affords all of our students a voice, and our end-of-semester student film screenings, which are attended by friends and families and other URI students and community members, assure that every student’s work is seen and heard.
We encourage our students to submit their work to film festivals, and, with the support of the Harrington School and the College of Arts & Sciences as well, Film/Media has been able to help students to attend important and prestigious festival screenings of their films.
We also are able to offer our students paid work in the Ranger Hall Media Equipment Center and as Student Assistants to Film/Media.
All available scholarships are awarded based on need.
The ethos of Film/Media is to form a cohesive working, creative and

14 inquiring community--and the center of that is the foundational practice of the importance, equality, opportunity, and dignity of every member of our community.
Strategy #3: Create an active learning community among students, faculty, staff, and administrators that engages in open discourse and enhance understanding about what it means to be a diverse and socially just community.
As an interdisciplinary major, FLM offers courses from Africana Studies and Gender and Women’s Studies, including the cross-listed ENG/AAF 352, Black Images in Film.
Studies in French, Italian and Spanish cinemas also count towards completion of the major, and have focused on Hispanic, Carribean, LatinX, and Maghreb filmmakers.
In the Fall of 2020, FLM faculty joined in a co-teaching project with Professors from Theatre and Honors to offer a section of AAF 300: Challenging Racism Through Film and Theatre.
This special topic course investigated the relation between race and theatre, and how racial issues have impacted on, or have, in turn, been affected by theatrical/filmic representations of race.
We are certainly hoping to offer this course again in the future.

Part of the gift of the FLM major is the ways in which our students work collaboratively on each other's films from beginning to end, and learn so much about each other in this process, as well as about the situations and topics around which their films are based.
Our diverse students are often tackling very personal subjects and reflecting on their histories and their lives in ways that intimately open up realities and lived experiences to other students.
Filmmaking--and discussions about the films that we watch and analyze together--is often difficult, as film leaves no topic unopened and ultimately excludes no one from the conversation, and Film/Media assures our commitment to that goal.
Film/Media has a small, but diverse faculty.
Our hope is to maintain equitable representation in not only the films that we include on our syllabi, but in promoting the ways in which the production of the moving image is not only a locus of international and global realities and creative endeavors, but a discipline that must ensure that all voices are heard and that all voices are afforded the opportunity to speak and be seen.

Our current position request for a potential future hire asks for an Assistant Professor of Production & Post-Production, specifically with a record of work that addresses issues of race, social and/or economic inequity and social justice.
Creating a Department of Film/Media should afford us a stronger chance of having this hire--and future diverse hires-- funded.
It is a goal of FLM to not only forefront the moving image as a reflection and focus of international and global realities and creative endeavors, but to also ensure that we are a part of the project that actively ensures that the film/TV and media industries move constantly towards social justice, equity, and diversity.
